query: For phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys, what single intervention could improve glass-forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous state? Formulate one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention without presupposing its class, the mechanism by which it would act, the predicted improvement relative to an otherwise comparable baseline, the conditions under which it should or should not work, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount (1–5 at.%) of boron to phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys will enhance their glass-forming ability and increase the thermal stability of their amorphous state.
generation.material_initial_state: A phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy (e.g., Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20) synthesized via arc melting and rapidly quenched using melt-spinning to yield an amorphous structure.
generation.intervention: Incorporate 1–5 at.% boron into the alloy composition.
generation.conditions: Alloys are produced under identical rapid solidification conditions (melt-spinning) with all parameters held constant except for the boron addition; experiments are conducted under conditions where cooling rates are sufficiently high to produce amorphous structures.
generation.structural_mediator: Preferential bonding between boron and phosphorus that disrupts crystalline nucleation.
generation.mechanism: The boron forms stable boron-phosphorus bonds that inhibit the formation of phosphorus-centered crystalline nuclei, thereby increasing the free energy barrier for crystallization. This stabilization of the supercooled liquid expands the glass-forming window and raises thermal transition temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: The boron-modified alloy will exhibit an increased glass transition temperature (Tg) and a higher onset temperature for crystallization compared with the baseline alloy. Additionally, improved glass-forming ability will be indicated by a wider supercooled liquid region and more robust amorphous microstructural stability.
generation.baseline: The phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy without any boron addition, produced under identical rapid quenching conditions.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected within the tested boron concentration range (1–5 at.%) and under rapid cooling conditions; if the element added has insufficient affinity for phosphorus or if the cooling conditions deviate significantly, the improvement may not be observed.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of thermal stability enhancement and the optimal boron concentration remain uncertain until tested. Additionally, potential side effects on other properties, such as mechanical ductility, are not fully known.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of baseline phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy and one set with 1–5 at.% boron addition, using identical melt-spinning conditions. Characterize both sets using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to determine the glass transition temperature (Tg) and crystallization onset. Complement thermal data with X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to verify the amorphous state and assess structural stability.
measurements: DSC curves to assess the width of the supercooled liquid region
XRD patterns for amorphous versus crystalline phases
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-added samples do not show a statistically significant increase in Tg or a higher crystallization onset temperature (i.e., a wider supercooled liquid region) compared to the baseline alloy, or if XRD and TEM reveal similar or more pronounced crystallinity in the boron-modified alloys, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Cooling rates significantly influence the microstructure and phase composition of the Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy. Slow cooling after arc melting results in a complex microstructure comprising multiple crystalline phases such as FCC “A”, tetragonal “B”, “C”, “D”, and orthorhombic “E”, while faster cooling after a short electric arc pulse reduces the number of phases to primarily FCC “A” and tetragonal “D”. Very rapid cooling using the melt-spinning method results in an amorphous structure, as confirmed by XRD and TEM analyses. Phosphorus addition enhances the alloy’s glass-forming ability during rapid cooling. The amorphous structure observed in the melt-spun ribbon demonstrates that the combination of phosphorus and high mixing entropy promotes the formation of amorphous phases during extremely fast cooling. However, further studies are necessary to understand the influence of phosphorus on mechanical properties and limitations, such as reduced ductility. To investigate the impact of small concentrations of an additionally added element on a glass-forming alloy, the critical cooling rates and glass formation regions are computed for the Pd-Ni-P-system micro-alloyed with 1 at% of Co, Cu, Fe, and Gd. Micro-alloying of Co, Cu, and Fe had little effect on the overall glass-forming ability which matches well with experimental results for (Pd40Ni40P20)99Co1 and (Pd40Ni40P20)99.4Fe0.6 that showed an impact on the mechanical properties without affecting the glass formation properties in a significant way (see Figure 6) [,]. This behavior is to be expected within the framework of the current model since cobalt, copper, and iron are similar in atomic weight and radius to nickel and therefore will not impact the calculation. This is different for gadolinium, since it varies in its properties significantly from the former alloying elements. The impact of the micro-alloying of gadolinium is even noticeable for concentrations below 1 at% as shown in Figure 6 within the employed model.

chosen.why: This move directly addresses the open question by inverting the current gap: while previous studies examined a fixed phosphorus-containing complex alloy, this study tests whether a targeted, minor compositional modification—using a well-established synthesis method—can enhance amorphous stability and glass formation. It leverages standard techniques and controlled changes in alloy chemistry to provide a clear, falsifiable hypothesis.
